source.title: TOAST: Transformer Optimization using Adaptive and Simple Transformations
source.authors: Irene Cannistraci; Simone Antonelli; Emanuele Palumbo; T. Sutter; E. Rodolà; Bastian Rieck; Julia E. Vogt

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures similarities between blocks within individual pretrained models, not alignment between independently trained models, convergence across seeds, or alignment that rises with model scale or capability. Its discussion cites cross-model alignment work but does not test those claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports within-model block-similarity analyses and block-approximation results. These concern a related but different construct from the claim versions, which concern alignment across independently trained models, models across seeds, or shared features across models. The paper also cites prior work on cross-model alignment and stitching; those cited findings are not rows.
record.test_reason: TOAST measures within-model block-to-block linear approximation error and uses intra-network redundancy as a tool for compression. It reports only its own method's accuracy and efficiency. It never compares independently trained models, seeds, modalities, or scales, so no claim version is tested. Its motivation cites cross-model alignment and stitching work as background, so 'uses_without_test'/T4 fits better than 'discusses'/T6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that pretrained transformers show consistent, model-determined intra-network block similarities. They also conclude that whole blocks can be replaced training-free by linear maps or the identity, cutting parameters and compute with small or no accuracy loss. A linear map often matches or beats trained MLP approximators. They draw no conclusion about cross-model convergence.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce the methods in the stated original sources; it measures within-model block similarity and uses it for block approximation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported within-model block-similarity patterns differ across architectures and are largely consistent across datasets for a given model; the paper says differences in values become more pronounced with more complex datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Within-model block-pair linear approximation error shows block-wise patterns. These differ across architectures and are largely consistent across datasets, with the block structure sharper on more complex datasets (Figs 2, 6). Layer-wise replaceability is architecture-dependent; base models tolerate single-block linear replacement better than small ones (Tables 13, 14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within pretrained vision transformers, adjacent blocks are often near-linearly related. The pattern is set mainly by the model rather than the data, and is more tolerant of replacement in larger models.

record.peer_reviewed: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (published 04/2026 in the text)
record.problems: For the claim versions, there are no cross-model, cross-seed, cross-modal, or scale comparisons. The recorded block-similarity figures provide no exact values in the text, and the study is primarily empirical.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted detailed CKA/representation comparisons after block approximation (Figure 3 and Figures 7–11), as well as block-replacement accuracy and efficiency tables: these concern within-model approximation or downstream task performance, not the cross-model convergence versions in the claim. The text describes some of these findings qualitatively, including model- and dataset-dependent approximation effects.

untested.parts: No cross-model alignment as a function of scale or capability. The finding that bigger models tolerate block skipping better is within-model.
No image-caption or vision-language alignment. The OpenCLIP experiment only approximates blocks of the vision encoder.
Seeds vary only the linear probe, not network initialization.
Linear maps are fitted between blocks of the same model, not between different models.
No features or circuits are compared across models.
The metric ablation (Table 11) compares block-selection metrics within a model, not cross-model convergence.
No cross-model alignment levels or causes are examined.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none'] and cannot_determine; they are within-model measures and are figure-only. Relation/tranche are changed from discusses/T6 to uses_without_test/T4, because the paper relies on intra-network representational similarity as a tool and reports only its own method's performance. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No comparisons of independently trained models across scale, capability, architecture, objective, or data.
No paired image-caption comparison or cross-modal alignment analysis.
No independently initialized seeds are compared for shared features or subspaces.
Mappings are fitted between blocks within one model, not between models or their representations.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are compared across models.
The paper compares candidate block-selection metrics, but does not test cross-model convergence across metrics, settings such as neighbour count, or in-distribution versus out-of-distribution inputs.
No cross-model alignment plateau or effects of shared training data or objectives are tested.

relation.reason: The abstract and related work discuss cross-model alignment and stitching, but the method uses intra-network redundancy rather than cross-model convergence.

tranche.reason: TOAST exploits similarity between blocks within one network, a different construct from convergence across independently trained models. It neither tests nor uses any listed claim version; cross-model alignment appears as related work.

source_check.notes: All sampled rows concern within-model block similarity and correctly link to no claim version. Table 8 identifies DINO-S and DINO-B as DINOv2 checkpoints; the figure values are appropriately left unquantified.
